findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATIONS, MEASURED (2): the duplicatePut fault class -- one of only two of criterion 1's five classes the row claims IS modelled -- is recorded but never observably injected. (a) I deleted the re-PUT at FaultInjectingStore.java:157, leaving the branch as `injected.add(new Injected("duplicatePut", key));` and nothing else: all 6 tests GREEN (`./gradlew :sequencer:test --tests binjava.sequencer.FaultInjectingStoreTest --rerun-tasks --no-build-cache`, BUILD SUCCESSFUL). The decorator then reports a duplicate it did not perform. Nothing in aDuplicatedPutIsHarmlessBecausePutIfAbsentIsWriteOnce can see the difference: `putIfAbsent` returns empty because MemoryBinStore already holds the key (true with or without the retry), `injected()` is non-empty because the add survives, and "B-got-here-first" survives BECAUSE NOTHING WAS WRITTEN rather than because the retry lost. (b) `return first;` -> return the DUPLICATE's result also survives all 6: on a FREE key the first PUT wins (present) and the retry loses (empty), so the decorator would tell the caller it lost a write-once slot it actually owns -- an I1 fabrication manufactured by the harness itself. The taken-key fixture cannot reach (b) at all. Kill (a) by observing the DELEGATE (the repo already has CountingBinStore) and asserting the key received TWO putIfAbsent attempts; kill (b) with a free-key case asserting the returned Version is present while `injected()` shows duplicatePut fired. Note the SAME shape on putIfMatch was a round-1 finding and was fixed and pinned (I verified: removing that landing kills anAmbiguousPutIfMatchALSOLands); this is the adjacent door left open.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor 'simplifies' the duplicate branch -- hoisting the two identical `new Body(...)` constructions into a local, or dropping the retry as apparently redundant since putIfAbsent is write-once anyway -- and the class silently degrades to a bookkeeping entry. M4.13 then runs 1,000 seeds and reports 'each fault class had a seed where it changed the outcome' for duplicatePut on the strength of `injected()`, which is the one signal that stays true when nothing is injected. The file's own javadoc names this exactly: 'a seed that silently injects nothing is a green test that proves the absence of testing'.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATIONS, MEASURED (2): the independence of the three fault streams -- the property the backlog row cites a MEASUREMENT for (two classes co-firing on draw 1 in 4,778 of 100,000 runs against ~250 expected under `seed*3+k`) -- is pinned by NOTHING but the comment at FaultInjectingStore.java:98-110. (a) I replaced the whole splitmix64 `scramble` body with `return seed * 3 + stream;`: all 6 tests GREEN. The fix for a defect the row says was measured re-opens verbatim with the suite green. (b) `fires` -> `if (p == 0.0) { return false; } return draws.nextDouble() < p;` -- i.e. exactly the early return the field javadoc at :72-83 says must not exist because it re-aligns every other class's faults when one is toggled: all 6 tests GREEN. Neither half of the stated property has a falsifier. Both are T0-testable with no store at all: (a) hold the seed fixed and assert the co-firing count of two classes over N seeds sits inside a band the linear scramble is outside of (the row already has the numbers); (b) hold the seed fixed, record the unreachable fault positions with duplicatePut=0 and with duplicatePut=0.5, and assert the unreachable positions are IDENTICAL. The three tests that do pass constrain only that the streams are seeded and seed-dependent -- `scramble` -> `return 99L` and `new Random(scramble(...))` -> `new Random()` both die on theSameSeedInjectsTheSameFaults, which is a much weaker property than decorrelation.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone finds splitmix64's three magic constants unexplained and replaces `scramble` with something readable -- `seed * 31 + stream`, `Objects.hash(seed, stream)`, or a single shared Random with the stream folded into the key -- and the suite stays green. Criterion 1's method (hold the seed, toggle one class, observe the outcome change) then attributes to the toggled class a difference caused by re-phasing the other two, and M4.13's per-class report describes one coin wearing three hats. The row's own measurement is the evidence that this is not hypothetical.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: there is NO test that `Faults` rejects an out-of-range probability -- say plainly: none. I deleted the entire compact-constructor guard (the `if (!(p >= 0.0 && p <= 1.0)) throw ...` body, leaving `check` empty): all 6 tests GREEN. The guard carries an eight-line javadoc calling itself 'rung 1 of gate-design' and naming the exact failure it prevents, and nothing anywhere in the diff can tell it apart from an empty method. Its BOUNDARIES are pinned only incidentally, by fixtures that happen to pass 0.0 and 1.0: I measured `p >= 0.0` -> `p > 0.0` killing 5 of 6 tests. So the accept path is constrained by accident and the REJECT path -- the only reason the guard exists -- is constrained not at all. Also unpinned: NaN, which the `!(...)` form deliberately rejects and which a naive `p < 0 || p > 1` rewrite would silently accept. One `assertThatThrownBy(() -> new FaultInjectingStore.Faults(-0.1, 0, 0)).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)` plus a NaN case kills both.
findings.failure_scenario: A later sweep is written as `new Faults(rate - margin, rate, rate)` or the probabilities are read from a system property, and one goes negative or NaN. The guard has meanwhile been removed as untested defensive code, or rewritten as `Math.clamp`/`p < 0 || p > 1` by someone tidying it. That class is then silently disabled for the whole sweep while `injected()` still shows the other two firing, so M4.13's aggregate 'faults fired' assertion stays green over a range that never exercised the class it was written for -- the risk the guard's own javadoc quotes.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATIONS, MEASURED (2), and a coherence problem: SimulatedClock is staged with NO test and NO staged caller. (a) `advance` body -> no-op: BUILD SUCCESSFUL. (b) `millis()` -> `return System.currentTimeMillis();`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Either mutation destroys the class's entire stated purpose ('a clock the simulation ADVANCES ... `Thread.sleep` would trade determinism for wall-clock time, which is what makes a failing seed a flake instead of a regression') and nothing in the tree notices. I confirmed by grep that the ONLY reference to SimulatedClock outside its own file is CommitProtocolSimulation.java:81, which is UNTRACKED and deliberately unstaged (M4.20) -- so in the tree this commit would create, the class is unreachable, untested code. The backlog row this diff writes claims M4.12 'keeps the FAULT-INJECTION LAYER only (FaultInjectingStore, SimulatedClock and THEIR TESTS)'; there is no SimulatedClockTest, and `check-tdd` cannot notice, because a class with no test demands no red record. Either add the ~4-line test (construct at 1_000_000, assert millis() and instant(); advance(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); assert both moved by exactly 5000 and NOT by wall time) or move the file to M4.20 where its consumer lives. The staged tests do NOT depend on any unstaged file -- I checked every import and reference in all three staged java files -- so the rest of the piece is self-contained; this class is the one part that is not.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.20 lands on top, its takeover-by-TTL-lapse path calls `clock.advance(ttl.plusSeconds(1))`, and `advance` has been made a no-op by a refactor (or `millis()` reads the wall clock after someone 'simplifies' the field away). The lease never expires on the simulated timeline, so every failover in the sweep silently reverts to the polite `close()` path -- the exact case the javadoc says the class exists to avoid -- and the sweep reports I1-I5 holding across 1,000 seeds having never once exercised an involuntary failover. With the wall-clock variant the failure is worse: seeds stop replaying and a real violation becomes a flake.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: `Injected.key` is never asserted anywhere. I rewrote every `new Injected("kind", key/k/p)` to `new Injected("kind", "")`: all 6 tests GREEN. Every assertion goes through `.extracting(Injected::kind)` or `kindsFor(...)`, which maps to kind only, so half the record is unconstrained -- including in theSameSeedInjectsTheSameFaults, whose replay comparison is over the kind sequence alone and would not notice a run that faulted different KEYS in the same order. `containsExactly` on the whole `Injected` record (kind and key) in the two single-fault tests, and comparing the full `injected()` list in the replay test, closes it.
findings.failure_scenario: A downstream assertion is written as 'this seed faulted the LEASE object, not a delta' by filtering `injected()` on key. The key has meanwhile been passed wrongly -- `list`'s branch already records the PREFIX rather than a key, so the two are not the same kind of string -- and the filter matches nothing, so the assertion passes vacuously by finding no counterexample.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATIONS, MEASURED (6): most of the decorator's surface is unconstrained. Each of these left all 6 tests GREEN: delete the unreachable branch from `stat` (:168-174); from `get` (:176-182); from `list` (:208-215); `getRange(k, a, b)` -> `getRange(k, b, a)` (argument swap, :185); `delete(keys)` -> dropped entirely (:218); `return List.copyOf(injected)` -> `return injected` (:120). Only `putIfAbsent` and `putIfMatch` are exercised at all -- deleting putIfAbsent's unreachable branch DOES die (anInjectedFaultCHANGESWhatTheCommitLogDoes), which incidentally proves CommitLog reaches putIfAbsent before any stat/get/list, i.e. that those three branches are unreached by the whole staged suite. A single test per faulting method (unreachable=1.0, assert IOException and one `Injected` with the right kind) plus a pass-through test for getRange/delete would cover it, all T1 on MemoryBinStore.
findings.failure_scenario: Two ways. (1) A silently dropped `delete` or a swapped `getRange` range makes the simulated store diverge from a real one, so the sweep validates the protocol against a store that does not behave like S3 and a genuine defect is never reached. (2) The unreachable branches on stat/get/list are what model criterion 1's 'partitioned leaders' on the READ path; if one is deleted or its `injected.add` dropped in a refactor, recovery and discovery become infallible in the simulation while the report still claims the class was exercised, and the aggregate count hides it because putIfAbsent's branch keeps firing.
